decisions.quote:
To this end, our analyses built on previous work by Hille and Schupp (2015) aiming to

replicate their findings. Contrary to the precursor study, our main results indicate a long-term

association with cognitive skills, but not with academic achievement. Further, our analyses

suggest that openness, conscientiousness, and perceived control are all positively associated

with musical participation, thus corroborating and expanding previous findings (e.g., Corrigall

et al., 2013).

decisions.reason: The abstract statement quoted in the shipped row affirms a broad positive association between musical training and non-musical skills rather than an overall replication verdict on Hille and Schupp (2015). When directly comparing their results to the precursor study, the authors explicitly contrast their cognitive skill and academic achievement findings while corroborating personality associations, which is mixed. Parent primary-source confirmation: The actual Hille/Schupp findings are independently identified in the Introduction: higher academic achievement, conscientiousness and openness among musicians. Current Results/Discussion retain conscientiousness/openness associations but contradict the broad academic-achievement result (with some German-grade subgroup agreement). Agreement is therefore not borrowed solely from Corrigall2013. The primary paper itself inconsistently describes prior perceived-control findings in Introduction versus Discussion; neither version is needed to force a categorical outcome. Actual original-specific agreement and disagreement support mixed.
